THE DETECTIVE MINDSET

Why read an article like a detective?

You’re not just reading for answers. You’re looking for clues.

✓
01 / DECIDEKnow quickly if it’s relevant.

Spot whether the article actually fits your research question or interests—before reading every page.

◈
02 / UNDERSTANDUnderstand it. Remember it.

Strategic reading helps you make sense of the study and remember what it says.

⌕
03 / DISCOVERFind other good articles.

The article you’re reading contains clues—keywords, references, and ideas—that lead to more research.

LOOK FOR CLUES → MAKE CONNECTIONS → FOLLOW THE EVIDENCE
STRATEGIES FOR READING & UNDERSTANDING ARTICLES

How to Read a Scholarly Article

You don’t have to read it from beginning to end! Start with what matters most.

1. Title & AbstractStart here. The abstract summarizes the research question, methods, and main findings.Ask: Is this study relevant to my question?
2. Discussion & ConclusionJump to the main takeaway: what the findings mean, why they matter, and any limitations.Ask: What did the researchers learn?
3. ResultsExamine the findings, tables, and figures. You don’t need to understand every statistic.Ask: What evidence supports the conclusions?
4. MethodsCheck how the study was done: participants, surveys, experiments, or other approaches.Ask: How trustworthy is this evidence?
5. Introduction & Literature ReviewReturn for background: what was already known and what gap the study addresses.Ask: What conversation is this study joining?

the anatomy of an article →

One Article Can Lead You to More

Look for clues in the article — then use them to understand what it’s about, decide if it’s relevant, and find other articles.

Illustrative scholarly article · Example for practice

Later School Start Times and
Sleep Patterns in Adolescents

Sample authors · Educational example

Abstract

This study examined the effects of later school start times on sleep duration and daytime functioning in high school students. Using a quasi-experimental design, researchers compared sleep patterns and academic performance at schools with different start times. Results suggested improvements in sleep duration and alertness among students at later-start schools.

Introduction

Adolescent sleep patterns are influenced by biological, social, and environmental factors. Earlier studies connect insufficient sleep with learning and well-being. Related concepts include circadian rhythm and sleep quality.

References

Earlier studies about adolescent sleep health and school start times offer paths to more research.
